results.message: So you'd agree the Donatists were just schismatics who deserved what they got?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
The Donatists were a separate communion, with their own bishops and altars in the same towns as ours. That much is a schism to us: not a mere argument, but a tear, when arguing stops and a new altar appears. Whether they deserved what they got is not a question we settle with one answer. In our later years Augustine moved across three stages on the matter. By his own later account, he first held that no one should be forced into the church. Later, he and his colleagues asked the emperors for a narrow measure. It was not granted. A broader law reached the same end first. Later still, he defended a fuller compulsion at length, when it was already in force. What moved him, he says, was pastoral experience of the Donatist schism. We hold it as his, argued at real length, and we hold it beside his first view, that no one should be forced. We do not call it plainly right, and we do not hide it either.

The sharpest question between us and them was the font. Is a baptism given outside the church's boundary valid? Cyprian held that nothing valid is given outside. Augustine held that something real is given even there, though it does the person no good until they come inside. Augustine wrote: “The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give ‘the form of godliness.’ Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.”

citations.sentence: In our later years Augustine moved across three stages on the matter.

sources.label: Augustine's three-phase development on coercion -- an early opinion against any compulsion (Letter XCIII §17), a narrow and unsuccessful solicitation of legal protection (Letter 185 §§25-26, earlier in his own episcopate), and finally a sustained defence of compulsion already in force -- records a genuine change of mind, reached through pastoral experience of the Donatist schism, rather than a retrospective self-presentation constructed after the fact to make an already-settled practice look like the outcome of principled reconsideration.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

glosses.plain_meaning: We argue hard, and we stay. Schism is the other thing: when arguing stops, and a new altar and a new bishop appear in the same town.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, schism means a split in the one church: someone leaves its clergy and people and sets up another altar. It is a tear, not a mere argument.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear denominational difference -- a normal, unremarkable feature of a plural religious landscape. We mean a tearing of a single body, with real consequences for standing, sacraments, and ordinary life in a town where both parties are present -- not one option among many, but the outcome we organize ourselves to avoid.
false_friend: a normal, unremarkable feature of a plural religious landscape, carrying no great weight

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

sentences.sentence: Augustine wrote: “The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give ‘the form of godliness.’ Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.”
sentences.why: quote placed by code, verbatim to its record

This term record IS that synthesis, so its own formation_confidence follows the synthesis's own rating, not the underlying quoted facts' rating. Doc_03 itself characterizes the pattern the same way: inferred from both bishops' conduct across more than one text, not a term either bishop names as such.

How this world characterizes its own opponents -- the Donatists specifically -- belongs to a later, separate step and this world's eventual Representative, not to this lexicon; this entry names the general concept only and does not characterize Donatism. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, of the type Application to this world, secondarily Historical scope. It runs over whether the heresy/schism distinction was as stable in this period as later usage implies, and how far the category describes a real ecclesial situation as against a polemical instrument used by the side that eventually prevailed. The North African case is the field's own central example. The entry does not present the distinction as a neutral technical taxonomy, and it does not settle whether the application of the category to rivals was accurate.

references.label: Augustine's three-phase development on coercion -- an early opinion against any compulsion (Letter XCIII §17), a narrow and unsuccessful solicitation of legal protection (Letter 185 §§25-26, earlier in his own episcopate), and finally a sustained defence of compulsion already in force -- records a genuine change of mind, reached through pastoral experience of the Donatist schism, rather than a retrospective self-presentation constructed after the fact to make an already-settled practice look like the outcome of principled reconsideration.

sources.locus: Letter 185, §§25-26, the imperial-coercion defence, directly quoted and re-verified
